Bac kground a nd
aims
This study evaluated
the
safety
and eﬃcacy
of
catheter ablation
in
treating atrial
brillation (AF)
among the
elderly












population.
. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
Met hods a nd
results
A
total
of 170
017 AF
ablation
procedures prospectively enrolled from 482
facilities
between 2017
and
2020
were















analysed. They were stratied into six age groups, ranging from < 65 to ≥85 years, in 5-year increments. A cut-oﬀ of 80

years was set for dividing participants into two groups. The primary endpoints included procedure-related complications
and 1-year arrhythmia recurrence after a 3-month blanking period. Patients ≥80 years constituted 7.2% of procedures
in 2017, which signicantly increased to 9.6% by 2020 ( P < 0.001). This older group predominantly comprised women
with smaller stature and body mass index,
a higher
prevalence of
paroxysmal
AF,
and a higher
rate of
initial ablation





procedures. The overall complication rate was 2.8%,
showing a positive correlation
with
age
( P < 0.001), peaking at




4.3%
for
patients 85
≥ years.
Older age
remained signicant
a
independent risk factor
for complications
(odds ratio:





1.36 [1.24,
1.49], P < 0.001). Cardiac tamponade, ischaemic stroke,
and sick sinus syndrome
were
more common in






the elderly. The recurrence rate
in the total population was
16.0% and did not diﬀer signicantly between age groups




(log-rank P = 0.473), remaining consistent even after adjusting for multiple variables.
. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
Conclusion
Although age increases complication risk, recurrence rates remained steady across age groups, suggesting that AF ablation
is a reasonable option for elderly individuals, contingent on careful patient selection for safety.

What is known :
r

prevalence of

brillation (AF) has been

Introduction
In recent
years, the
prevalence of
atrial
brillation (AF) has been
















increasing.
1
Owing to
the
strong relationship between age
and
AF









development,
2
the number of patients with this arrhythmia will con-
tinue to increase as the population ages, making the management of
elderly patients
with
AF a pressing concern.
Catheter ablation
has














become an increasingly popular option for managing AF in the elderly
population. For example, in Japan, the proportion of patients aged 75
years or older
among those who received
this treatment increased


from 8.5% in 2011 to 20.8% in 2017,
3 , 4
though the national guideline
published recommended a more
cautious approach to treatment in

older patients compared with younger individuals.
5
Consequently, it is
essential to evaluate the appropriateness of the increasing use of this
invasive
treatment
in
the
elderly population, given
the
limited data










on its
safety and eﬃcacy for this age group.
Hence, at the Japanese

Heart Rhythm Society (JHRS), we analysed data from the Japan Abla-
tion Registry (J-AB), a nationwide, prospective registry that is jointly

6
to
assess the safety and eﬃcacy of AF ablation in the elderly population
by comparing the frequency of complications and AF recurrence rate
in very elderly patients with those in younger patients.
Methods
Data source
The cohort analysed in this study
was obtained from the J-AB registry,


a prospective nationwide multicentre registry established by the JHRS in
collaboration with the National Cerebral and Cardiovascular Center in

Osaka, Japan.
6
Participation in this registry is mandatory for arrhythmia-
training facilities accredited by the JHRS. In Japan, implantable cardioverter
debrillator and AF ablation procedures using balloon ablation technology
can only be performed at facilities accredited by the JHRS. The registry’s
inclusion criterion was procedures involving catheter ablation for cardiac
arrhythmia.
Surgical management procedures for
arrhythmias
were ex-
cluded from this registry. Data on the following parameters were collected:
patients’
background (age, sex, and
underlying
heart diseases); type
of







targeted arrhythmia; acute outcome of
the procedure; and acute com-


plications, including bleeding complications (Bleeding Academic Research
Consortium type 3 or 5),
7
cerebral infarction, transient ischaemic at tack ,
systemic embolisms, phrenic
nerve paralysis, oesophageal
injury,
peri-







carditis, sick sinus syndrome, atrioventricular block, and in-hospital death
(cardiac, non-cardiac, and unknown) during hospit alization. Det ails of com-
plications
were
mandatory
for all cases, and the safety analysis cohort



was composed of all registered patients who had valid data. Detailed data
collection was performed every September, including patient background,
medication, and procedural outcomes ( Supplementary material online,






Figure S1). The procedures performed in September,
for which these











procedural outcomes were collected, constituted the eﬃcacy analysis









cohort. Considering the potential impact on data comprehensiveness due
to the researcher’s workload, we collected
detailed
data
exclusively on

procedures conducted in September. After obtaining consent and approval
from the local institutional review board committee of the participating
instructions, the physician sent a registration form to the J-AB secretariat
at the National Cerebral and Cardiovascular Center. All data registration
was conducted via the web using the Research Electronic Data Capture
system. All compiled data remained anonymous, even to registry coordina-
tors , and cont ained no patient-identifying information. The annual reports
for 2018, 2019, and 2020 have been published.
8 –10
The study was conducted in 2017 in accordance with the Declaration
of Helsinki and the Ethical
Guidelines for Clinical Studies issued by the







Ministry of Health, Labour, and Welfare, Japan. Furthermore, it was ap-
proved by the
institutional review board of
the
National Cerebral and


Cardiovascular Center, Japan, along with the institutional review boards
of all participating institutions and registered with the UMIN Clinical Trial


Registry (UMIN000028288) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03729232). All





participants provided informed consent and were free to withdraw their
consent at any time.
Study population
Data on AF ablation procedures performed from January 2017 to Decem-
ber 2020 were analysed. Among the 232 161 catheter ablation procedures
performed
during this period
in
482 facilit ates , dat a on AF ablation










procedures and possible errors
were extracted. A ow chart of the











patient selection process is shown in Figure 1 . Finally, 170 017 AF ablation
procedures were included in the safety study. The eﬃcacy analysis
was

performed using 1-year follow-up data collected more
by
detailed data

collection, which was performed only in September of each year. Overall,
18 319 procedures performed in September were included in this study.
Of these,
13 551
were AF ablation
cases,
and 11 358
cases
for which

follow-up data were available were analysed for AF recurrence.
Safet y a
nd eﬃc acy outcomes

Safety
outcomes and the incidence of
procedure-related
acute







complications during each patient’s hospitalization period were evaluated.
We dened a complication as an unexpected medical problem that









occurs during or after a procedure. The protocol specied that clinically
meaningful complications
requiring intervention
were
to
be reported.








Complications
were
sub-classied
into puncture-site
complications,








cardiac tamponade/pericardial eﬀusion, other bleeding complications,





symptomatic stroke/transient ischaemic attack, oesophagus-related




5182.23988Page 4
326
K. Inoue et al.



complications, phrenic nerve palsy, sick sinus syndrome, and in-hospital
death.
Eﬃcacy outcomes were assessed based on recurrent arrhythmias after
ablation. Follow-ups after ablation were performed according to the stan-
dard of care at each institute. Freedom from recurrence was dened as
1-year freedom from AF/atrial tachycardia/atrial utter > 30 s beyond a
3-month blanking period.
St atistic a l a
na lysis

The study population was stratied into six groups according to age at
the time of the AF ablation procedure: ≤64, 65–69, 70–74, 75–79, 80–84,
and ≥85 years. The participants were divided into two
groups with a









cut-oﬀ age of 80 years for multivariate analysis and comparison of the

incidence of each
complication. Cases with missing or potentially erro-



neous data were not entirely excluded. Specically, any pairs containing
missing or erroneous data were omitted from analyses that required









paired
values.
Furthermore, when
dealing
with
individual
variables with

missing values, the missing data points were excluded from the associated
calculations . Supplementary material online, Table S1 delineates the pro-





portion of absent data corresponding to each variable across the distinct
age cohorts. Despite the missing entries within the dataset, there were no
pronounced biases or systematic tendencies within their dispersion that
could have compromised the validity of the analytical outcomes. Continu-
ous variables are reported as medians (interquartile range), and categorical
variables are presented
as
numbers
(percentages). Analysis of variance,

the Kruskal–Wallis test, and the chi-square test were performed to test
the signicance of diﬀerences between age categories for continuous and
categorical variables, respectively. To assess the trend of complications



across age groups, the Cochran–Armitage trend test was conducted. To

investigate the risk of procedure-related complications and recurrence,

multivariable logistic regression models were used and adjusted for vari-
ables that yielded a P -value of < 0.1 in the univariate analysis. In addition, to
investigate the diﬀerences in recurrence with standard- of- care monitoring,
univariate and multivariable survival analyses were conducted between the
age subgroups. To compare the risk of complication, inverse probability of

treatment weighting (IPTW) was also performed to adjust for potential
confounders and balance covariates between patients over 80 years old
receiving AF ablation and the younger patient cohort. The Kaplan–Meier
analysis was performed using the log-rank test for age-based classication.
Statistical signicance
was dened as a P -value of < 0.05. All
statistical











analyses were performed using STATA version 16 (St at a Corp, College
Station, TX, USA).

Study population to evaluate safety




outcomes
We identied 170 017 catheter ablation procedures for AF performed
between
January
2017
and
December 2020.
The median
ages of












the patients who received
this treatment
in 2017, 2018, 2019, and







2020
were
67, 68, 69,
and
69
years,
respectively,
with the
patient














age
increasing signicantly with
time (
P < 0.001). Moreover,
the












demographic composition of the patients undergoing this procedure
showed a marked and continuous increase in the number of older in-
dividuals: the percentage of patients aged 75 years or higher increased
from 20.8% in 2017 to 23% in 2018, 25.3% in 2019, and 27.3% in 2020.
Meanwhile, the proportion of those aged 80 years or higher increased
from 7.2% in 2017 to 7.2% in 2018, 8.4% in 2019, and 9.6% in 2020
( P < 0.001) ( Figure 2 ).
Patient characteristics are shown in Table 1 . The median age of the
patients was 69 years, and males accounted for 69.6% of the total. The
mean patient body weight was 65 k g , and the mean body mass index
was 23.9.

Age and complications
Procedure-related complications were reported in 2.78% of the study
population.
The complication
rates
for each
age subgroup
were as





follows: 2.27% for < 65, 2.61% for 65–69, 2.84% for 70–74, 3.50% for
75–79, 3.47% for 80–84, and 4.30% for those aged ≥85. There was a
signicant positive association between age and the complication rate
( P -value for the trend < 0.001). Figure 3 shows a forest plot comparing
the complication risks between the age groups. The complication rate
increased with age, with no distinct threshold observed in procedures
for patients aged > 65 years. In the multivariate analysis, after adjusting
for sex, body mass index, number of sessions, coronary artery disease,
hypertrophic cardiomyopathy,
dilated
cardiomyopathy,
and valvular





heart disease, older age remained an independent and signicant risk
factor for procedure-related complications ( Table 2 ). Using IPTW for
covariate adjustment, our analysis revealed a higher complication risk
in patients
over 80 undergoing AF
ablation compared with younger

individuals, with age
≥ as
80
a
signicant
factor [odds ratio
(OR)












1.25 (95% CI 1.13–1.39), P < 0.001] ( Supplementary material online,


Table S3).

Discussion
This study evaluated the safety and eﬃcacy of AF ablation in elderly
patients using data from a prospective nationwide multicentre registry
dat abase cont aining over 170 000 AF ablation cases. The key ndings
of this study are as follows. There was a considerable increase in the
percentage of patients aged ≥80 years who underwent AF ablation,
from 7.2% in 2017 to 9.6% in 2020. The complication rate increased
with age, with
no distinct
threshold
observed in procedures

Elderly patients and AF ablation



In our
study, patients
aged 80
≥ years constituted 8.4%
of the total


sample. Given
the
number
of elderly
patients
with
AF,
we
deduced


that only a small proportion of patients underwent AF ablation. There
were several
signicant
diﬀerences in patient
backgrounds between


the age groups. Among
patients aged
< 65 years, the majority were


male (82.3%), whereas, in
the
group aged
≥ years, the
85
majority









were female (53.4%). This sex
discrepancy
may reect
the marked





diﬀerence in lif
e expectancy in
Japan
(81.5
years for
men
and
87.6









years for women in 2019), where the study was conducted.
15
The me-
dian height and weight of the ≥85 years age group were 154 cm and
53 k g , respectively. Despite
their predominantly Asian backgrounds,

the elderly
individuals
undergoing
ablation were
relatively
small
in









stature. This disparity was more pronounced in the group aged < 65
years (height and weight: 170 cm and 72 k g , respectively).
The
high


prevalence of underlying
cardiac
diseases suggests
that they are a












high-risk patient group. More cases involved rst-time ablation, parox-
ysmal AF, and instances in which no approach other than pulmonary
vein isolation was
used.
It is important to note
that the inclusion

















criteria and ablation strategies employed may have varied among the
participating centres. Nonetheless, our ndings suggested that when
conducting AF
ablation in elderly patients,
the practitioners tend to


select early-stage AF cases and employ simplied ablation strategies,
considering the associated risks of the procedure. These patient and
procedure selections may
be important
for preserving safety in
the





elderly population.
Aging and complication risk

Our study found a statistically signicant correlation between age and
the complication rate. When patients were stratied into two groups
using
the
age of 80
years as
a cut-oﬀ, older age
remained
a signi-





cant predictor of complications after adjustments in the multivariate
analysis. However, the OR was 1.21
(1.11–1.33),
which
may not be




substantial. Our study also demonstrated that age was a risk factor for
specic complications but not for others. The prevalence of cardiac
tamponade in older
individuals
is likely
attributable
to age-related













anatomical changes and tissue fragility. This nding is consistent with
the fact that age is considerably associated with symptomatic stroke,
transient ischaemic attack, and sick sinus syndrome, which are not lim-
ited to patients with AF. In-hospital mortality was signicantly higher
among
the elderly than
among
the non-elderly patients (0.16% vs.










0.05%; P = 0.001).
Compa rison wit h previous studies



regarding complications

Previous meta-analyses have compared complication rates between
age groups
17 –19
; however, one limitation observed across studies has
been the lack of consistent age thresholds. Nevertheless, these analy-
ses consistently indicated that age was a risk factor for complications.
13652.639679999997Page 9
Catheter ablation for AF in very elderly patients
331





This study contributes signicantly to this understanding by including
a subgroup of patients aged ≥85 years and demonstrates that there
is no clear tipping point in complication rates as age increases, made
possible
by
collecting
many cases
using
the same criteria. Another







study analysed the large Japanese Diagnosis Procedure Combination
(DPC) database,

20
which enables epidemiological studies targeting






specic populations due to its extensive
medical
data.
However,












because the database is
primarily
used
for medical
expense
claims,



physicians can freely assign diagnostic
labels, potentially
leading to












inaccurate diagnoses and data quality issues that may introduce bias
into
the analytical
results. Current prospective
registration
studies










are generally considered to have higher data reliability than the DPC
database analyses. Additionally, the number of cases in our study was
higher
than that
in
the
DPC
database analysis. We also
conducted



eﬀectiveness analyses that were not possible with the DPC database.
The similarities in the complication rates and tendencies between the
two studies suggested that the results of each analysis were valid.
Aging and recurrence


Our study found no
signicant
diﬀerences in
the
recurrence rates














among the age-stratied groups. Given
the considerable diﬀerences

between groups in factors associated with recurrence, such as sex,
21
type of AF,


22
and body weight,
23
we made
adjustments
in
the mul-
tivariate analysis. Age was not a risk factor for recurrence. Although
there may be selection bias and the analysis might be underpowered
to detect miniscule diﬀerences in eﬃcacy despite the large sample size,
these ndings suggest that catheter ablation could be a viable option
for rhythm management in selected elderly patients.

regarding recurrence

age has
traditionally
been
regarded as a risk













factor
for
AF
recurrence, with
some models incorporating it
as
a














variable to predict AF
recurrence,






24 –27
recent
meta-analyses
have



yielded inconsistent ndings.




17 –19 , 28
Our
analysis demonstrated
no




discernible
increase
in
the
recurrence rate in elderly patients.
The













discrepancy between the studies may
be
attributable
to diﬀerences



in patient
characteristics and
selection
criteria.
In our investigation,







an extensively higher proportion of
early-stage
AF
cases, such as












those involving initial procedures and paroxysmal AF, were observed
in older cohorts, which may have resulted from the patient selection.
The most notable strengths of
this
prospective
registry study were
its extensive sample size and the inclusion of a substantial number of
patients over the age of 85, a population rarely reported in previous
research. On the other hand, implementing a uniform
and stringent

monitoring
method for
recurrences is
extremely
diﬃcult in
such










an extensive nationwide
registry. The standard- of- care monitoring







during follow-up used in this study could lead to an underestimation
of the recurrence rate compared with more rigorous monitoring such
as implantable loop recorder.
Therefore, it would be
inappropriate






to
compare the
rates
with those
of
other
studies.
Nevertheless,









considering
the
consistent
methodology
employed
throughout the






study,
we
deemed it
appropriate
to
compare
outcomes
among









age subgroups
within the same
cohort.
Consequently, the lack of










diﬀerence in recurrence rates observed in our data suggests
that

















appropriate patient selection should be performed in
real-world












settings when conducting AF ablation in elderly patients.
Appropriateness of AF ablation in the





elderly
Previously, complication incidence rates were signicantly higher com-
pared to current levels. For instance, in a worldwide survey conducted
in 2010, the overall study population reported incidence rates of 4.6%
for all complications, 0.94% for ischaemic stroke/transient ischaemic
at tack , and 1.3% for cardiac tamponade.
29
Our previous study based
on the Japan Catheter Ablation Registry of AF, which we conducted
before the initiation of the J-AB study, showed that the incidence rates
of these complications in the total cohort in 2011 were 5.8%, 0.3%,


and 1.1%, respectively.
3
However, the corresponding rates improved
to 3.4%, 0.04%,
and
0.8%, respectively, in 2017.











4
In
this
study,
the



corresponding rates of these complications in patients aged ≥80 years
were 3.6%, 0.27%,
and
1.0%, respectively. While age is a
signicant







risk factor for complications, it is
noteworthy that the complication
rate
among the
subgroup aged
≥ years
80
in our study was
lower













than that
in
the total
cohort from a
decade
ago,
which
can be















attributed to the swift improvement in complication rates over time.
Given that the relatively high complication rate reported 10 years ago
was considered
acceptable
at
the time,
it may be
inappropriate
to









conclude that catheter ablation is unsuitable for elderly patients based
solely on the higher complication rate compared with that in younger
patients . Nevertheless , when contemplating
the
implement
ation of











ablation in elderly patients, it is important to note that perioperative
mortality
among the demographic
is
signicantly
higher
compared







with that among younger
individuals.
Moreover, it is imperative to














consider
variables that are salient
risk factors
for complications
in











the
elderly age group,
such as
low body weight
and
long-standing















persistent AF.
Our data
revealed no discernible
increase
in
the recurrence rate




of AF
among
elderly patients. Considering
that
factors related to















recurrence tend to
increase with age, these
ndings suggest
that












appropriate patient selection is necessary in real-world settings when
performing
ablation
in elderly patients
with
AF.
Furthermore, this










nding implies that rhythm management with AF ablation is a viable
therapeutic option for specic elderly patients.
Limitations
This study has few limit ations . First, despite utilizing a vast prospective
real-world registry dataset
for analysis, the
coverage rate
for
AF











ablation in
Japan
is estimated to be
∼
90% of
the Japanese
DPC
















database,
30
potentially introducing bias in patient enrolment. Second,
because ablation for AF is invasive
and costly, only a select group of

elderly patients can receive it. Hence, the data should be interpreted
with the understanding that this study had a selection bias. Third, as
this
study focuses on a
Japanese
population,
adapting
its nding to










European or
North American
populations, where obesity is more













prevalent, may be challenging. This aspect warrants further research.
Fourth, although patient selection is presumed to be crucial for achiev-
ing favourable outcomes with ablation in the elderly population, our
analysis does not provide insights into the specic criteria or methods
for optimal patient selection.
Fifth, the
observed recurrence rate












highly depended on the arrhythmia monitoring strategy; however, the
strategies varied between the practices. Furthermore, the standard-


of-care monitoring during follow-up could lead to an underestimation
of
the
recurrence
rate, as
discussed
above. Sixth, this
study
cap-










tured procedure-related acute
complications; hence,
delayed-onset








complications were not assessed, such as atrial-oesophageal stula or
PV stenosis. Seventh, patients who underwent multiple procedures








during the registration period may have been
registered more than



once. Consequently, the impact of
these
patients could be greater










than that of those who received only
a single treatment. Finally, this

study evaluated
the appropriateness
of
catheter ablation for
AF in










the elderly only in terms of safety and eﬃcacy and not in its entirety.
For example, cost-eﬀectiveness is
another crucial
aspect, given
the






relatively high expenses
associated with this treatment modality. Al-

though AF
ablation
is expected to improve
the
prognosis in some













patients, its impact on
the
elderly
remains unclear. Furthermore,











quality-of-life considerations in
the decision-making
process
for
AF







15346.719639999996Page 10
332
K. Inoue et al.



ablation in the elderly were not addressed. This study did not investi-
gate these aspects because the data required for such analyses were
unavailable.
Conclusion
Age was a
signicant
risk factor of
complications, although the












observed complication rates in the elderly population were not dis-
proportionately high.
The
recurrence rate in elderly patients was















comparable with that in younger
patients. Therefore, while prudent

patient selection and a judicious treatment strategy are essential for
safety concerns, AF
ablation
is a
reasonable treatment
option
for












elderly individuals.
